Here's an implementation of the logic in React using JavaScript. This version assumes a web-based environment where the status of tasks is managed through a frontend, and the validation logic runs within the React component. The code uses state to manage the assignor status and assignee progress, and it will display a modal or alert when an invalid combination is detected.

React Implementation of Task Status Monitoring

This example uses a simple approach with React, and for displaying messages, we'll use a basic alert. You can replace this alert with more sophisticated modals from libraries like React-Bootstrap, Material-UI, or similar for a better user experience.

 

 

import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Function to check status combination validity
const checkStatusCombination = (assignorStatus, assigneeProgress) => {
 // Define invalid combinations with reasons and next actions
 const invalidCombinations = {
   'Open-In Progress': {
     reason: 'Task cannot start without being reviewed; no set duration or start date.',
     solution: 'Prevent task from moving to In Progress without being reviewed.',
     nextAction: 'Review the task and set the status to Reviewed.',
   },
   'Open-Testing': {
     reason: 'Testing cannot occur without prior review and task progress.',
     solution: 'Ensure the task is Reviewed and worked on before Testing.',
     nextAction: 'Review the task and update the assignee progress correctly.',
   },
   'QA-Not Started': {
     reason: 'QA cannot occur on tasks that haven’t shown any progress.',
     solution: 'Disallow QA status without task progressing through work phases.',
     nextAction: 'Ensure the task reaches In Progress or Testing first.',
   },
   'Completed-Assigned': {
     reason: 'Task cannot be marked as Completed while still in the Assigned phase.',
     solution: 'Ensure the task progresses through appropriate stages before completion.',
     nextAction: 'Move through In Progress, Testing, and QA phases before setting to Completed.',
   },
   // Add other invalid combinations as needed
 };

 // Construct the key to check in the dictionary
 const key = `${assignorStatus}-${assigneeProgress}`;

 // Check if the combination is invalid
 if (invalidCombinations[key]) {
   const { reason, solution, nextAction } = invalidCombinations[key];
   // Display an alert or replace this with a modal
   alert(
     `This status & progress combination is not allowed. Reason: ${reason} Solution: ${solution} Next Action: ${nextAction}`
   );
 }
};

const TaskStatusMonitor = () => {
 // State to hold the current status values
 const [assignorStatus, setAssignorStatus] = useState('Open');
 const [assigneeProgress, setAssigneeProgress] = useState('Assigned');

 // Handler for status change
 const handleStatusChange = () => {
   // Check the combination whenever statuses are updated
   checkStatusCombination(assignorStatus, assigneeProgress);
 };

 return (
   <div>
     <h2>Task Status Monitor</h2>

     {/* Dropdown for Assignor Status */}
     <label>
       Assignor Status:
       <select
         value={assignorStatus}
         onChange={(e) => setAssignorStatus(e.target.value)}
       >
         <option value="Open">Open</option>
         <option value="Reviewed">Reviewed</option>
         <option value="QA">QA</option>
         <option value="Completed">Completed</option>
         <option value="Closed">Closed</option>
       </select>
     </label>

     {/* Dropdown for Assignee Progress */}
     <label>
       Assignee Progress:
       <select
         value={assigneeProgress}
         onChange={(e) => setAssigneeProgress(e.target.value)}
       >
         <option value="Assigned">Assigned</option>
         <option value="Not Started">Not Started</option>
         <option value="In Progress">In Progress</option>
         <option value="Waiting Action">Waiting Action</option>
         <option value="Testing">Testing</option>
         <option value="Completed">Completed</option>
         <option value="Rework">Rework</option>
       </select>
     </label>

     {/* Button to trigger status check */}
     <button onClick={handleStatusChange}>Check Status Combination</button>
   </div>
 );
};

export default TaskStatusMonitor;
=======================

Code Explanation:

  1. State Management:
    • The component manages the assignorStatus and assigneeProgress using the useState hook.
  2. Checking Combinations:
    • The checkStatusCombination function is called whenever the statuses are changed, checking if the current combination is valid.
  3. Invalid Combinations:
    • A dictionary of invalid combinations (invalidCombinations) is used to store the invalid combinations, their reasons, solutions, and next actions.
  4. Displaying Alerts:
    • If an invalid combination is detected, an alert is displayed with detailed information. For a production system, replace alert with a more user-friendly component like a modal.
  5. Dropdown Menus:
    • Dropdown menus allow the user to select the current assignor status and assignee progress. This simulates how statuses might be updated in a real-world task engine.
  6. Button to Trigger Validation:
    • A button is provided to manually check the status combination, simulating a real-time validation check within the application.

Next Steps:

  • Replace Alerts: For a better user experience, replace the alert function with a modal or notification system in React.
  • Integrate with Backend: If statuses are updated in real-time from a backend, connect this logic to automatically validate whenever a status change is detected.
  • Error Handling: Add additional error handling as needed to ensure the system gracefully handles unexpected values.

461.content:
To integrate the task status monitoring system with a backend, you'll need to set up a backend service that can handle status updates, validate combinations, and send feedback to the frontend. Below are the steps to add backend integration using Python (Flask) for the backend and React for the frontend. This integration will allow status updates to be processed and validated centrally.

Backend Setup: Using Flask (Python)

Step 1: Setting Up the Flask Backend

  1. Install Flask:

    • If you haven't installed Flask yet, you can install it using pip:

      bash

      pip install flask

  2. Create a Flask Server:

Create a file named app.py for the backend server.

  • Flask Backend Code (app.py):

 

 

from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
from flask_cors import CORS

# Initialize the Flask app
app = Flask(__name__)
CORS(app)  # Enable CORS to allow requests from your frontend

# Define invalid status combinations with reasons, solutions, and next actions
invalid_combinations = {
   ('Open', 'In Progress'): {
       'reason': 'Task cannot start without being reviewed; no set duration or start date.',
       'solution': 'Prevent task from moving to In Progress without being reviewed.',
       'next_action': 'Review the task and set the status to Reviewed.'
   },
   ('Open', 'Testing'): {
       'reason': 'Testing cannot occur without prior review and task progress.',
       'solution': 'Ensure the task is Reviewed and worked on before Testing.',
       'next_action': 'Review the task and update the assignee progress correctly.'
   },
   ('QA', 'Not Started'): {
       'reason': 'QA cannot occur on tasks that haven’t shown any progress.',
       'solution': 'Disallow QA status without task progressing through work phases.',
       'next_action': 'Ensure the task reaches In Progress or Testing first.'
   },
   ('Completed', 'Assigned'): {
       'reason': 'Task cannot be marked as Completed while still in the Assigned phase.',
       'solution': 'Ensure the task progresses through appropriate stages before completion.',
       'next_action': 'Move through In Progress, Testing, and QA phases before setting to Completed.'
   },
   # Add more invalid combinations as needed
}

@app.route('/check-status', methods=['POST'])
def check_status():
   """
   Endpoint to check if the status combination is valid.
   Receives JSON data with assignorStatus and assigneeProgress.
   """
   data = request.json
   assignor_status = data.get('assignorStatus')
   assignee_progress = data.get('assigneeProgress')

   # Check if the combination is invalid
   combination = (assignor_status, assignee_progress)
   if combination in invalid_combinations:
       details = invalid_combinations[combination]
       # Return the reason, solution, and next action as a JSON response
       return jsonify({
           'allowed': False,
           'reason': details['reason'],
           'solution': details['solution'],
           'nextAction': details['next_action']
       }), 400
   else:
       # Return that the combination is valid
       return jsonify({'allowed': True}), 200

if __name__ == '__main__':
   app.run(debug=True)
 

======================================

Frontend Setup: Using React

  1. Set Up React to Connect to Flask Backend:

    • Install axios to handle HTTP requests from React to the Flask backend:

      bash

      npm install axios

  2. Update React Component to Include Backend Call:
  • Modify the TaskStatusMonitor component to send requests to the Flask backend.
  1. React Code with Backend Integration:

=============

 

import React, { useState } from 'react';
import axios from 'axios';  // Import Axios for HTTP requests

const TaskStatusMonitor = () => {
 // State to hold the current status values
 const [assignorStatus, setAssignorStatus] = useState('Open');

 // Function to handle status checks by communicating with the backend
 const handleStatusChange = async () => {
   try {

     const response = await axios.post('http://localhost:5000/check-status', {
       assignorStatus,

     });

     // If the combination is valid, notify the user
     if (response.data.allowed) {
       alert('The status and progress combination is allowed.');
     }
   } catch (error) {
     // If the combination is not allowed, display the reason and suggested actions
     if (error.response && error.response.status === 400) {

       alert(
         `This status & progress combination is not allowed. Reason: ${reason} Solution: ${solution} Next Action: ${nextAction}`
       );
     } else {
       alert('An error occurred while checking the status combination.');
     }
   }
 };

 return (
   <div>
     <h2>Task Status Monitor</h2>

     {/* Dropdown for Assignor Status */}
     <label>
       Assignor Status:
       <select
         value={assignorStatus}
         onChange={(e) => setAssignorStatus(e.target.value)}
       >
         <option value="Open">Open</option>
         <option value="Reviewed">Reviewed</option>
         <option value="QA">QA</option>
         <option value="Completed">Completed</option>
         <option value="Closed">Closed</option>
       </select>
     </label>

     {/* Dropdown for Assignee Progress */}
     <label>
       Assignee Progress:
       <select
         value={assigneeProgress}
         onChange={(e) => setAssigneeProgress(e.target.value)}
       >
         <option value="Assigned">Assigned</option>
         <option value="Not Started">Not Started</option>
         <option value="In Progress">In Progress</option>
         <option value="Waiting Action">Waiting Action</option>
         <option value="Testing">Testing</option>
         <option value="Completed">Completed</option>
         <option value="Rework">Rework</option>
       </select>
     </label>

     {/* Button to trigger status check */}
     <button onClick={handleStatusChange}>Check Status Combination</button>
   </div>
 );
};

export default TaskStatusMonitor;
 

===

Steps to Connect Frontend and Backend:

  1. Run the Flask Backend:

    • Start the Flask server using:

      bash

      Copy code

      python app.py

  2. Run the React Frontend:

    • Make sure your React app is running using:

      bash

      Copy code

      npm start

  3. Testing Integration:
    • When you change the statuses in the dropdowns and click "Check Status Combination," the React frontend will send the status data to the Flask backend.
    • If the combination is invalid, the backend responds with an error message that includes the reason, solution, and next action, which is then displayed to the user in the frontend.

Additional Integration Tips:

  • CORS Configuration: Ensure your Flask backend allows requests from your React frontend using CORS.
  • Error Handling: Implement robust error handling to manage unexpected backend failures or network issues.
  • Scaling Up: As the system grows, consider deploying the backend on a cloud server and adjusting the endpoints accordingly.

462.content:
To enhance the user experience, modals are a great alternative to alerts for displaying messages, especially when guiding users through task status issues. Below, I'll show you how to integrate a modal into the React application to replace the basic alert functionality.

We'll use the React-Bootstrap library, which provides easy-to-use components, including modals. You can also use other libraries like Material-UI or build custom modals, but React-Bootstrap offers a straightforward approach for this example.

Step-by-Step Guide to Implement Modals in React

Step 1: Install React-Bootstrap and Bootstrap

First, you need to install React-Bootstrap and Bootstrap CSS in your React project.

bash

 

npm install react-bootstrap bootstrap

Add the Bootstrap CSS to your index.js or App.js file:

javascript

 

// Add this import to your main entry point (index.js or App.js) import 'bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css';

Step 2: Update the React Component to Use a Modal

Here’s the updated code that uses a modal instead of an alert. This example assumes that invalid status combinations are validated by calling the Flask backend as described earlier.

 

import React, { useState } from 'react';
import axios from 'axios';  // Axios for HTTP requests
import { Modal, Button } from 'react-bootstrap';  // Import Modal and Button from React-Bootstrap

const TaskStatusMonitor = () => {
 // State to hold the current status values
 const [assignorStatus, setAssignorStatus] = useState('Open');
 const [assigneeProgress, setAssigneeProgress] = useState('Assigned');
 
 // State to manage the modal visibility and content
 const [showModal, setShowModal] = useState(false);
 const [modalContent, setModalContent] = useState({
   title: '',
   reason: '',
   solution: '',
   nextAction: ''
 });

 // Function to handle status checks by communicating with the backend
 const handleStatusChange = async () => {
   try {
     // Sending a POST request to the backend to check status validity
     const response = await axios.post('http://localhost:5000/check-status', {
       assignorStatus,
       assigneeProgress,
     });

     // If the combination is valid, notify the user (you could also add a success modal here)
     if (response.data.allowed) {
       setModalContent({
         title: 'Valid Status',
         reason: 'The status and progress combination is allowed.',
         solution: '',
         nextAction: ''
       });
       setShowModal(true);
     }
   } catch (error) {
     // If the combination is not allowed, display the reason and suggested actions
     if (error.response && error.response.status === 400) {
       const { reason, solution, nextAction } = error.response.data;
       setModalContent({
         title: 'Invalid Status Combination',
         reason: reason,
         solution: solution,
         nextAction: nextAction
       });
       setShowModal(true);
     } else {
       // Handle unexpected errors
       setModalContent({
         title: 'Error',
         reason: 'An error occurred while checking the status combination.',
         solution: '',
         nextAction: ''
       });
       setShowModal(true);
     }
   }
 };

 // Function to close the modal
 const handleClose = () => setShowModal(false);

 return (
   <div className="container">
     <h2>Task Status Monitor</h2>

     {/* Dropdown for Assignor Status */}
     <label>
       Assignor Status:
       <select
         value={assignorStatus}
         onChange={(e) => setAssignorStatus(e.target.value)}
         className="form-control"
       >
         <option value="Open">Open</option>
         <option value="Reviewed">Reviewed</option>
         <option value="QA">QA</option>
         <option value="Completed">Completed</option>
         <option value="Closed">Closed</option>
       </select>
     </label>

     {/* Dropdown for Assignee Progress */}
     <label>
       Assignee Progress:
       <select
         value={assigneeProgress}
         onChange={(e) => setAssigneeProgress(e.target.value)}
         className="form-control"
       >
         <option value="Assigned">Assigned</option>
         <option value="Not Started">Not Started</option>
         <option value="In Progress">In Progress</option>
         <option value="Waiting Action">Waiting Action</option>
         <option value="Testing">Testing</option>
         <option value="Completed">Completed</option>
         <option value="Rework">Rework</option>
       </select>
     </label>

     {/* Button to trigger status check */}
     <Button variant="primary" onClick={handleStatusChange}>
       Check Status Combination
     </Button>

     {/* Modal for displaying status validation results */}
     <Modal show={showModal} onHide={handleClose}>
       <Modal.Header closeButton>
         <Modal.Title>{modalContent.title}</Modal.Title>
       </Modal.Header>
       <Modal.Body>
         {modalContent.reason && <p><strong>Reason:</strong> {modalContent.reason}</p>}
         {modalContent.solution && <p><strong>Solution:</strong> {modalContent.solution}</p>}
         {modalContent.nextAction && <p><strong>Next Action:</strong> {modalContent.nextAction}</p>}
       </Modal.Body>
       <Modal.Footer>
         <Button variant="secondary" onClick={handleClose}>
           Close
         </Button>

David  to meet David , understand an create  Screen based Daily task 

 

To effectively view a specific assignee's daily tasks along with their current statuses, you can implement a filtering system that allows you to filter tasks based on the assignee, task statuses, and dates. Here's a method that will help you efficiently track and review the tasks:

Step-by-Step Guide to Filter Daily Tasks for a Specific Assignee

  1. Use Existing Filters on Fields:
    • Utilize the filter options that are available on the fields in your task engine, as seen in the attached image. These filters allow you to narrow down tasks based on various criteria like assignee name, task status, start date, due date, and other relevant fields.
  2. Implement a Date Range Filter:
    • Add or use the existing date filters to set a specific range (e.g., Today, This Week). This will help in focusing only on tasks relevant for the specific day you want to review.
  3. Filter by Assignee:
    • Use the filter on the "To" or "Assignee" field to select the specific person whose tasks you want to view. This will display only the tasks assigned to that individual.
  4. Filter by Status:
    • Use the filter on the "Assignee Progress" field to select relevant statuses. You can select:
      • Reviewed → Not Started
      • Reviewed → In Progress
      • Reviewed → Waiting Action
      • Reviewed → Testing
      • Reviewed → Completed
  5. Combine Multiple Filters:
    • Combine filters to narrow down to exactly what you need:
      • Assignee: Filter by the specific person.
      • Status: Filter by statuses that indicate the work in progress or review phases.
      • Date: Set the filter to show tasks for today or a specific day.
  6. Sort by Start Date or Due Date:
    • Sort the tasks by Start Date to see which tasks are scheduled to begin today.
    • Alternatively, sort by Due Date to focus on tasks that need to be completed today.
  7. Duration/Time Estimation:
    • Use the Duration column (if available) to estimate how much time each task will take. This helps in planning the day efficiently.

Example Use Case: Viewing Daily Tasks

Let's say you want to see all tasks for "River Stewart" that are in progress for today:

  1. Set the Assignee Filter:
    • Filter "To" or "Assignee" field: River Stewart.
  2. Set the Status Filter:
    • Filter "Assignee Progress" field: Reviewed → In Progress.
  3. Set the Date Filter:
    • Set the Start Date or Due Date filter to Today’s Date.
  4. Review the Filtered Results:
    • You will see only today’s tasks for River Stewart that are currently in progress, along with their start and due times.

Benefits of This Approach:

  • Focused View: Provides a clear view of what tasks are assigned and what their current status is.
  • Time Management: Helps the assignee and manager track tasks efficiently, knowing which ones are pending, in progress, or waiting for action.
  • Actionable Insights: Quickly identify tasks that require input or need immediate attention, ensuring nothing falls behind schedule.

Possible Enhancements:

  • Save Filter Views: If your task engine allows it, save these specific filter settings as a custom view for quick access.
  • Daily Report Generation: Implement a feature to generate a daily task report for each assignee based on the filtered results.
  • Visual Indicators: Add color coding or icons to highlight tasks that are urgent or waiting for action.

Valid assign status & Assignee  progress 

 

 

 

  1. Task Creation:
    • Assignor issues the task and selects the best candidate.
    • Task automatically gets the status of "Open".
  2. Task Review and Planning:
    • Assignee and assignor review the task.
    • They set a start date and duration.
    • Status changes to "Reviewed".
    • If start date is within 24 hours or in the past, the task moves to "In progress" under active project.
    • If the start date is more than 24 hours in the future, task stays as "Not started/on track".
  3. Active Task Progress:
    • Assignee works on the task with status "In progress".
    • Assignee has three choices: a. Continue work (stays "In progress") b. Move to "Testing" (part of active task) c. Set as completed (automatically goes to Assignor QA)
  4. QA Process:
    • Assignor checks the QA section of active tasks.
    • Assignor has three options: a. Mark as complete (system changes status to "Completed") b. Set for rework (task goes back to "In progress") c. Continue QA (stays in QA status)
  5. Task Completion:
    • When a task under "Completed" is checked one final time: a. If approved, it's sent to "Closed" b. If issues found, it goes back to "In progress"
  6. Special Statuses:
    • "Pending for assignor input ": Used when there's an issue requiring the assignor to revisit the task.
    • "Pending for assignor input (assignee)": Used when the assignee cannot complete the task during their attempt and needs to flag it.
    • Both of these statuses indicate the task is blocked.

This flow now incorporates all the statuses from the image and addresses the additional points you've mentioned. The process includes the necessary interactions between assignee and assignor, and it enforces testing before completion.

Do you have any further adjustments or additions you'd like to make to this flow? Once you're satisfied with the flow, we can move on to discussing the specific features and user interface design for the task assignment app.

When Assignee sets "Pending for assignor input ":

Key Rules:

  • Task creation requires both Assignor and Assignee

  • Assignee status must be Completed before task can move to Done stage

  • Assignee cannot be in Testing before In progress

  • Assignor QA status only possible after Assignee Completed status

  • Closed status only possible after both parties mark as Completed

  • Either party can initiate a blocked state, but both cannot be blocked simultaneously

  • Blocked states can occur at any active stage of the task

Example

How the Assignee Can Use This Kanban Board with Past Due Indicators and Potential Automation to Manage Tasks Efficiently

Kanban Board Components:

  1. Columns: Each column represents a status (e.g., Open, Reviewed, QA, Completed, Closed, and Awaiting Input), which reflects the progress of tasks.
  2. Task Cards: These cards include key details:
    • Task Name: What the task is.
    • Assignee Progress: The current status of the task.
    • Priority: High, Medium, Low.
    • Start Date, Due Date, and Duration: Information that guides the assignee on when to start and finish the task.
    • Status Indicator: Tasks that are on track or past due are marked with appropriate color codes (e.g., red for past due).

Past Due Indicators:

Tasks with past due dates are highlighted in red. These are the most critical tasks and must be prioritized. The assignee can easily spot overdue tasks and take corrective action.

Using the Kanban Board Effectively

  1. Tracking Tasks by Status:
    • As an assignee, the tasks are automatically categorized by their progress. Tasks can move between columns such as Open, Reviewed, In Progress, QA, and more.
    • Past Due Tasks are highlighted, allowing the assignee to focus on them first.
  2. Managing by Dates (Start, Due, Duration):
    • Start Date: The assignee should begin working on the task on or before the start date.
    • Duration: The assignee must manage their time effectively based on the task duration, ensuring enough time for each phase (e.g., In Progress, Testing).
    • Due Date: The assignee must complete the task before the due date, moving the task to Testing or Completed as needed.
    • Tasks nearing or passing the due date will be marked Past Due on the board, prompting immediate action.
  3. Automation to Help with Past Due Tasks:
    • Automation features can notify the assignee when a task is past due, reminding them to prioritize those tasks.
    • Alerts can be set up to notify both the assignor and assignee when a task is nearing its due date to ensure proactive management.
    • Automated Task Reprioritization: The system can automatically move past due tasks to the top of the Kanban board or create an alert for tasks nearing their due date.
    • Daily Reminders: Automation can send daily or weekly summaries of tasks that are close to or past their due dates, allowing the assignee to stay on top of their workload.

Expanded Explanation of Transitions and Timelines

The board captures each transition in the task lifecycle, ensuring that the assignee is aware of the necessary timelines and when tasks move from one stage to another.

Assigning Task Duration, Start Date, and Due Date:

  • When the assignor creates a task, they assign the duration, start date, and due date. These parameters ensure that the task is completed within a set time frame.
  • As the assignee, it's crucial to:
    • Begin work on or before the start date.
    • Plan work based on the duration to ensure each step (In Progress, Testing, etc.) is completed before the due date.
    • Complete the task before the due date to avoid it becoming overdue.

QA → Rework → In Progress or Testing:

  1. In Progress:
    • If the task requires substantial changes after QA, the assignee moves the task to "In Progress" and continues working.
    • The task may stay within its original timeline, or the assignor may adjust the timeline if the changes are large.

 

==============================================>>>>>>>>

Additional Features of the Kanban Board:

  • Drag-and-Drop Functionality:
    • The assignor can drag tasks from one column to another based on their current status. For example, if a task moves from In Progress to Testing, it can be dragged to the appropriate column.
  • Task Cards:
    • Each task is represented as a task card in the Kanban board. Task cards display:
      • Task ID (for easy tracking)
      • Task Name (brief description)
      • Priority (e.g., High, Medium, Low)
      • Due Date (helps the assignor know which tasks are due soon)
      • Assigned To (assignee name, though this would usually be the same person in this context)
  • Filtering:
    • The assignor can filter the tasks on the board based on assignee, priority, or due date.
  • Comments and Notes:
    • Each task card could have a small icon or section for comments, so the assignor can leave notes or feedback for the assignee, such as requesting clarification or updates.
  • Color Coding:
    • High-priority tasks can be color-coded (e.g., red for urgent tasks) to draw attention.
    • Tasks close to their due date or overdue could also change colors to alert the assignor.

Benefits of Using a Kanban Board for Assignors:

  1. Visual Clarity: The assignor can see at a glance where all tasks are in the workflow, helping them prioritize and manage their time effectively.
  2. Task Monitoring: It's easy to monitor the progress of tasks without having to read through a list—tasks are visually grouped by status.
  3. Proactive Management: If a task is stuck in Waiting Action or Testing for too long, the assignor can intervene quickly to keep things moving.
  4. Quick Reassignment or Action: If priorities change, tasks can be easily reassigned or updated directly on the board.
  5. Daily and Weekly Overviews: Assignors can review progress at the beginning or end of each day/week to see which tasks need more attention or are nearing completion.

How an Assignor Might Use the Kanban Board:

  • Morning Check: At the beginning of the day, the assignor checks the In Progress and Waiting Action columns to see where input is required and what the assignee is working on.
  • Mid-Day Adjustments: The assignor might drag tasks between columns based on updates from the assignee, such as moving tasks to Testing once the work is done.
  • End-of-Day Review: At the end of the day, the assignor checks the Completed column to review tasks that are finished and ready for closure or QA.

Yes, GitHub 

 

offers built-in Kanban board functionality through GitHub Projects, which allows you to visually manage tasks using a Kanban-style board. However, if you are looking for Kanban board libraries to integrate into your own applications, GitHub hosts several open-source Kanban board libraries.

Option 1: GitHub Projects (Built-in Feature)

GitHub Projects allows you to create Kanban boards to manage issues, pull requests, and tasks across repositories. This feature is great for managing projects within the GitHub environment, offering:

  • Columns for tasks (To Do, In Progress, Done).
  • Cards representing issues, pull requests, and notes.
  • Drag-and-drop functionality to move tasks between columns.
  • Automated workflows to move cards based on issue status or commit activity.

How to Use GitHub Projects as a Kanban Board:

  1. Navigate to the repository or organization where you want to manage your project.
  2. Click on the Projects tab.
  3. Create a new project and select the Kanban board template.
  4. Add issues, pull requests, or notes as cards to the board.
  5. Move tasks between columns as their status changes.

This is ideal if you are managing a software development project on GitHub.

Option 2: Open-Source Kanban Libraries on GitHub

If you need to integrate a Kanban board into your own project or application, here are some popular open-source Kanban libraries available on GitHub:

1. react-kanban

  • Repository: react-kanban on GitHub
  • Description: A lightweight and flexible Kanban board built using React. It allows you to create and manage boards, columns, and cards with drag-and-drop functionality.
  • Features:
    • Drag-and-drop tasks between columns.
    • Customizable board and card design.
    • Support for task filtering and sorting.
    • Lightweight and easy to integrate into a React project.

  • Installation:

    bash

    Copy code

    npm install @lourenci/react-kanban

  • Usage:

    javascript

    Copy code

    import Board from '@lourenci/react-kanban'; import '@lourenci/react-kanban/dist/styles.css'; function KanbanBoard() {  const board = {    columns: [      {        id: 1,        title: 'To Do',        cards: [{ id: 1, title: 'Task 1', description: 'Task description' }],      },      {        id: 2,        title: 'In Progress',        cards: [],      },    ],  };  return <Board initialBoard={board} />; }

  • Use Case: Perfect for React applications that need a customizable Kanban board.

2. Vue-Kanban

  • Repository: vue-kanban on GitHub
  • Description: A Kanban board component for Vue.js. It is designed for Vue.js applications and offers drag-and-drop functionality.
  • Features:
    • Lightweight and easy to set up in Vue projects.
    • Full Kanban board functionality with drag-and-drop cards between columns.
    • Easily customizable with Vue components.

  • Installation:

    bash

    Copy code

    npm install vue-kanban

  • Usage:

    javascript

    Copy code

    import Vue from 'vue'; import Kanban from 'vue-kanban'; new Vue({  el: '#app',  components: { Kanban }, });

3. jKanban (Pure JavaScript)

  • Repository: jKanban on GitHub
  • Description: A Kanban board library built with vanilla JavaScript, making it suitable for any project without a framework dependency.
  • Features:
    • Pure JavaScript, no framework dependency.
    • Supports drag-and-drop functionality.
    • Customizable columns and cards.
    • Great for non-React or non-Vue projects.

  • Installation:

    bash

    Copy code

    npm install jkanban

  • Usage:

    html

    Copy code

    <div id="myKanban"></div> <script>  var kanban = new jKanban({    element: '#myKanban',    boards: [      {        id: '_todo',        title: 'To Do',        item: [{ id: '1', title: 'Task 1' }],      },      {        id: '_inprogress',        title: 'In Progress',        item: [],      },    ],  }); </script>

4. react-trello

  • Repository: react-trello on GitHub
  • Description: A fully customizable Trello-like Kanban board for React. It includes built-in features for managing tasks and workflows.
  • Features:
    • Drag-and-drop support for cards.
    • Easy to integrate into React applications.
    • Customizable and styled components.

  • Installation:

    bash

    Copy code

    npm install react-trello

  • Usage:

    javascript

    Copy code

    import Board from 'react-trello'; const data = {  lanes: [    {      id: '1',      title: 'To Do',      cards: [{ id: 'Card1', title: 'Card 1' }],    },    {      id: '2',      title: 'In Progress',      cards: [],    },  ], }; function KanbanBoard() {  return <Board data={data} />; }

5. Kanban (for Angular)

  • Repository: Angular Kanban on GitHub
  • Description: A simple, lightweight Kanban board for Angular projects. This is ideal if you're using Angular and need a Kanban-style task management system.
  • Features:
    • Supports drag-and-drop functionality.
    • Easy to set up in Angular apps.

  • Installation:

    bash

    Copy code

    npm install @hoatle/angular-kanban

Choosing the Right Kanban Board Library:

  • If you're using React: Use react-kanban or react-trello. Both are customizable and offer the functionality needed for creating Kanban boards within React applications.
  • If you're using Vue.js: Go for vue-kanban. It's lightweight and integrates seamlessly with Vue projects.
  • If you're using Angular: Consider Angular Kanban for integrating with Angular apps.
  • If you're using vanilla JavaScript: jKanban is a good option, with no dependencies on a specific framework.

Conclusion:

  • For GitHub Users: GitHub Projects' built-in Kanban functionality is a good choice for managing open-source or collaborative software development projects.
  • For Custom Applications: Choose a Kanban library based on the framework you're using (React, Vue, Angular, etc.). All of the mentioned libraries are open-source and well-maintained, making them excellent options for task management.

Let me know if you'd like further details on setting up any of these Kanban libraries!

Following is cut and past of Dialpad history , to AI and asking for important and relevant data . Once you have the pictures , then we will be 100 for 2 door project or more 

 

 

The discussion between David Khorram and Blue Hawk Technologies covers various technical aspects of installing an access control system at a site, focusing on integrating Kisi hardware with existing security infrastructure. Here's a detailed summary, structured by key topics discussed:

1. Existing Infrastructure & Compatibility:

  • Electric Strike: The site already has an electric strike installed on a metal glass door. Blue Hawk recommends utilizing this existing infrastructure, as it is already compliant with local city codes. This saves the effort of installing a magnetic lock, which would require additional work like tying it into the building’s fire alarm panel​​.
  • Code Compliance: It's mentioned that fire safety codes in Boca Raton, FL, require specific electrical panel connections, which would complicate adding magnetic locks. Utilizing the electric strike simplifies the installation​.

2. Hardware Recommendations:

  • Kisi Pro Readers: David confirms the use of Kisi Pro readers that require Cat6 cabling. Blue Hawk states that all cables, including the existing ones, will be replaced with new Cat6 cables​​.
  • Motion Sensors and Push to Exit: A motion sensor or push to exit (PTE) button will be added to meet the access control needs for exiting the premises​​.
  • Power Supply & Fire Alarm Integration: The Kisi power supply includes a connection to the fire alarm system. In case of fire, all doors will automatically unlock. However, fire alarm technicians from the building will be responsible for the actual connection​​.

3. Project Scope and Workflow:

  • Cabling and Low Voltage Work: Blue Hawk confirms that all low-voltage work, including Cat6 cabling for the Kisi readers and ethernet, will be handled by their team. There is a clarification about running new cabling for the reader, including powering the door strike​​.
  • Engineering Review: David plans to take the photos of the site and the discussed setup to his engineering team for review and scope of work confirmation before proceeding​​.

4. Risks & Concerns:

  • Battery Backup & Power Outages: David raises concerns about using magnetic locks in areas prone to power outages (e.g., during hurricanes in Florida). With magnetic locks, doors unlock when the battery depletes after 24 hours, posing a security risk. However, electric strikes remain locked in the absence of power, making them a safer option​​.
  • Door Durability: Blue Hawk warns against modifying the existing high-quality door to install a magnetic lock, stating it could compromise the integrity of the door. The electric strike is preferred for this reason​​.

5. Next Steps:

  • Blue Hawk will send photos of the site for further review by the engineering team.
  • David plans to finalize the scope, receive a quote from Blue Hawk, and pay 50% upfront to begin the project.
  • The discussion also hints at future expansions, including integrating cameras and using Kisi’s mobile phone access and face recognition capabilities for enhanced security​​.

6. Additional System Features:

  • Kisi Reader Pro & Controller Pro: These provide mobile app access control and cloud management. They eliminate the need for local servers and offer features like over-the-air updates, real-time event logs, and integration with security workflows. This simplifies the management of access control at multiple locations​​.

Conclusion:

The discussion centers around leveraging existing infrastructure (electric strike and cabling) to meet access control needs while maintaining compliance with fire safety codes. The team will use Kisi’s cloud-based access control system, integrating motion sensors, readers, and Cat6 cabling for a secure and manageable system. The overall goal is to keep the installation efficient, code-compliant, and minimize risks associated with power outages.

For further steps, you can proceed with:

  1. Estimate
  2. High-level proposal
  3. Formal proposal documentation
  4. Detailed planning process
  5. Implementation process

The door strike already installed is an electric strike. Based on the discussion, this strike is fail-secure, meaning that in the event of a power failure, the door remains locked unless power is supplied to it.

This type of electric strike, as confirmed by Blue Hawk Technologies, is configured to stay locked without power and only opens when power is applied. This behavior is preferred in areas like Florida, where power outages (e.g., during hurricanes) are common. The fail-secure configuration ensures that even during a prolonged outage, the door does not automatically unlock, maintaining security​​.

Proposal Longwood, Fl -   

1- Look at the spreadsheet and pricing , I am not sure our pricing is accurate check it with your suppliers

2- I got my info from the project + AI 

SOW: Hope you are both well! Florida is preparing for yet another hurricane and Paul raised a good question.

For our Longwood, FL location the main front door utilizes that door strike not maglock. In the event of a power outage (past the time of the backup battery allotment) – does the door’s deadbolt lock still function? We want to know what options at this site will allow us to ensure the front door stays locked even if the KISI system stops functioning completely.

We would like to get a backup battery at a minimum of this location ASAP that is for 48 hours. Can you send specs of a unit that would be best for this scenario?

 

For a 48-hour backup power solution for three maglocks, the power consumption and the type of backup system (like a UPS) will need to match the total power required by these maglocks.

Typically, each maglock requires around 300mA (0.3A) at 12V or 24V. Assuming you are using three maglocks at 12V, the total current required would be around 0.9A.

To maintain power for 48 hours, you'd need a UPS or battery backup system capable of delivering this power continuously for the full duration. Here’s a rough calculation:

  • Power for three maglocks: 0.9 A×12 V=10.8 W0.9 \, A \times 12 \, V = 10.8 \, W0.9A×12V=10.8W
  • For 48 hours: 10.8 W×48 hours=518.4 Wh10.8 \, W \times 48 \, hours = 518.4 \, Wh10.8W×48hours=518.4Wh

You’ll need a UPS or battery backup system that can provide at least 518.4 watt-hours (Wh). Given this calculation, a 600 Wh UPS or higher should suffice.

A suitable option could be a CyberPower PR750LCDRT1U UPS, which provides up to 750 VA / 600 watts of power. This would give enough capacity for your maglocks and other equipment if needed.

UPS proposal - Google Docs proposal

 We are working no our own custom verision of a text editor similar to CKEditor. Due to response length limitations in Claude, additional functionality will need to be added to the icons. Please enable functionality for every icon, and us CHatGPT 40 w/Canvas to debug and comment the code, ensuring every icon is functional.

 

See below code:

import React, { useRef, useEffect } from 'react';
import {
 Bold, Italic, Underline, Strikethrough,
 AlignLeft, AlignCenter, AlignRight, AlignJustify,
 List, ListOrdered, Link, Image, Undo, Redo,
 CheckSquare, Mic, Highlighter, Palette, Type,
 MoveDown, FileSpreadsheet, FileText
} from 'lucide-react';

const EnhancedTextEditor = () => {
 const editorRef = useRef(null);
 const fileInputRef = useRef(null);

 const applyFormatting = (command, value = null) => {
   document.execCommand(command, false, value);
   editorRef.current.focus();
 };

 const applyHeadingSize = (size) => {
   let tag;
   let style;
   switch (size) {
     case 'title':
       tag = 'h1';
       style = 'font-size: 2.5em; font-weight: 600;';
       break;
     case 'heading':
       tag = 'h2';
       style = 'font-size: 1.5em; font-weight: 500;';
       break;
     case 'normal':
       tag = 'p';
       style = 'font-size: 1em; font-weight: normal;';
       break;
     case 'small':
       tag = 'p';
       style = 'font-size: 0.8em; font-weight: normal;';
       break;
     default:
       tag = 'p';
       style = '';
   }
   document.execCommand('formatBlock', false, `<${tag} style="${style}">`);
   editorRef.current.focus();
 };

 const handleImageInsertion = (event) => {
   const file = event.target.files[0];
   if (file && file.type.startsWith('image/')) {
     const reader = new FileReader();
     reader.onload = (e) => {
       const img = document.createElement('img');
       img.src = e.target.result;
       img.style.maxWidth = '100%';
       img.style.height = 'auto';
       insertNodeAtCursor(img);
     };
     reader.readAsDataURL(file);
   }
 };

 const insertNodeAtCursor = (node) => {
   const selection = window.getSelection();
   if (selection.rangeCount) {
     const range = selection.getRangeAt(0);
     if (editorRef.current.contains(range.commonAncestorContainer)) {
       range.deleteContents();
       range.insertNode(node);
       range.setStartAfter(node);
       range.setEndAfter(node);
       selection.removeAllRanges();
       selection.addRange(range);
     } else {
       editorRef.current.appendChild(node);
     }
   } else {
     editorRef.current.appendChild(node);
   }
   editorRef.current.focus();
 };

 const insertCheckbox = () => {
   const checkbox = document.createElement('input');
   checkbox.type = 'checkbox';
   checkbox.style.marginRight = '5px';
   
   const span = document.createElement('span');
   span.appendChild(checkbox);
   span.appendChild(document.createTextNode('\u00A0'));
   
   insertNodeAtCursor(span);
 };

 useEffect(() => {
   editorRef.current.focus();
 }, []);

 return (
   <div style={containerStyle}>
     <div style={toolbarStyle}>
       <select onChange={(e) => applyHeadingSize(e.target.value)} style={selectStyle}>
         <option value="normal">Normal Text</option>
         <option value="title">Title</option>
         <option value="heading">Heading</option>
         <option value="small">Small Text</option>
       </select>
       <IconButton onClick={() => applyFormatting('bold')} tooltip="Bold"><Bold size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => applyFormatting('italic')} tooltip="Italic"><Italic size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => applyFormatting('underline')} tooltip="Underline"><Underline size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => applyFormatting('strikeThrough')} tooltip="Strikethrough"><Strikethrough size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => applyFormatting('justifyLeft')} tooltip="Align Left"><AlignLeft size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => applyFormatting('justifyCenter')} tooltip="Align Center"><AlignCenter size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => applyFormatting('justifyRight')} tooltip="Align Right"><AlignRight size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => applyFormatting('justifyFull')} tooltip="Justify"><AlignJustify size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => applyFormatting('insertUnorderedList')} tooltip="Bullet List"><List size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => applyFormatting('insertOrderedList')} tooltip="Numbered List"><ListOrdered size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => applyFormatting('createLink', prompt('Enter URL:'))} tooltip="Insert Link"><Link size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => fileInputRef.current.click()} tooltip="Insert Image"><Image size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={insertCheckbox} tooltip="Insert Checkbox"><CheckSquare size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => document.execCommand('undo')} tooltip="Undo"><Undo size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => document.execCommand('redo')} tooltip="Redo"><Redo size={16} /></IconButton>
       
       {/* New icons for future features */}
       <IconButton onClick={() => {}} tooltip="Speech Dictation"><Mic size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => {}} tooltip="Highlight Text"><Highlighter size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => {}} tooltip="Change Text Color"><Palette size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => {}} tooltip="Increase Font Size"><Type size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => {}} tooltip="Decrease Font Size"><MoveDown size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => {}} tooltip="Export as Excel"><FileSpreadsheet size={16} /></IconButton>
       <IconButton onClick={() => {}} tooltip="Export as Word"><FileText size={16} /></IconButton>
       
       <input
         type="file"
         ref={fileInputRef}
         style={{ display: 'none' }}
         onChange={handleImageInsertion}
         accept="image/*"
       />
     </div>
     <div
       ref={editorRef}
       contentEditable={true}
       style={editorStyle}
     />
   </div>
 );
};

const IconButton = ({ onClick, tooltip, children }) => (
 <div style={iconButtonContainerStyle}>
   <button onClick={onClick} style={iconButtonStyle}>
     {children}
   </button>
   <span style={tooltipStyle}>{tooltip}</span>
 </div>
);

const containerStyle = {
 fontFamily: '-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif',
 maxWidth: '800px',
 margin: '20px auto',
 backgroundColor: '#ffffff',
 borderRadius: '10px',
 boxShadow: '0 4px 6px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1)',
 overflow: 'hidden',
};

const toolbarStyle = {
 display: 'flex',
 flexWrap: 'wrap',
 gap: '5px',
 padding: '10px',
 backgroundColor: '#f0f0f0',
 borderBottom: '1px solid #e0e0e0',
};

const iconButtonContainerStyle = {
 position: 'relative',
 display: 'inline-block',
};

const iconButtonStyle = {
 padding: '8px',
 backgroundColor: '#ffffff',
 border: '1px solid #d1d1d1',
 borderRadius: '6px',
 cursor: 'pointer',
 transition: 'all 0.2s',
 ':hover': {
   backgroundColor: '#e6f2ff',
   color: '#007aff',
 },
};

const tooltipStyle = {
 visibility: 'hidden',
 backgroundColor: 'rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.7)',
 color: '#fff',
 textAlign: 'center',
 borderRadius: '4px',
 padding: '5px',
 position: 'absolute',
 zIndex: 1,
 bottom: '125%',
 left: '50%',
 transform: 'translateX(-50%)',
 opacity: 0,
 transition: 'opacity 0.3s',
};

const selectStyle = {
 padding: '8px',
 backgroundColor: '#ffffff',
 border: '1px solid #d1d1d1',
 borderRadius: '6px',
 cursor: 'pointer',
 fontSize: '14px',
};

const editorStyle = {
 border: 'none',
 minHeight: '200px',
 maxHeight: '600px',
 padding: '20px',
 fontSize: '16px',
 lineHeight: '1.5',
 overflowY: 'auto',
 outline: 'none',
};

export default EnhancedTextEditor;

554.content:
1. A user was getting an error message when trying to login. This was due to the password reset token expiring or becoming invalid. We need to fix this by making the error messages more easy to understand.

2. Upon first time accessing OneSurvey, it downloads the service worker which takes time, and this may be the reason that some people are having issues with logging in. Let's investigate further and review in the meeting

3. We also need to make it so the user does not need to copy and paste their username and temporary password.

 

First time login sequence should go as follows:

  1. Account manager sends invitation email
  2. New user receives email along with their username (no more temporary password)
  3. After clicking the Discover Beta button, it should go to the login page and ask the user to type in their username (this page would also provide an indicator that the username can be found in the invitation email)
  4. After click a button to set the password, it could bring the user to a page to enter their password
  5. As soon as the password is set, the user can click the button, and this would immediately log the user in, instead of forcing them back to the main login page to enter the username and new password again.

GPT SUGGESTIONS:

  • Invitation Email Clarity:
    • Including the username directly in the email is good, but ensure that the email also provides clear instructions that the username will be needed on the login page, along with a clear call to action for setting the password.
  • Set Password Flow:
    • Instead of asking the user to type their username again, you can prepopulate the username field after they click the invitation link. This eliminates redundancy and reduces friction.
    • On the "set password" page, ensure you implement strong password guidelines and provide immediate feedback on password strength. This helps the user pick a secure password from the start.
  • Seamless Login After Password Set:
    • Automatically logging the user in after they set their password is a good idea. It improves the user experience by reducing unnecessary steps. Ensure the system does proper session handling at this point to secure the login.
  • Optional Security Enhancements:
    • Consider adding a one-time use token in the invitation email. This token can be embedded in the link that, when clicked, verifies the user's identity and pre-fills their username on the login page. This avoids the user manually entering the username while ensuring that only the invited user can set up the account.
  • Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA):
    • After setting the password, you could optionally prompt the user to set up MFA to enhance security, especially if the system contains sensitive data.

    • Step 3: When the user selects text and clicks the "AI" icon, a modal window (pop-up) will appear, divided into two vertical sections.

      • Section 2 (right or below): List of available prompts, with a button for users to add their own prompt.
      • Admins should have the ability to delete or edit any prompt, while users can only add new prompts.
  5. Prompt Selection:
    • Step 5: When the user selects one of the prompts (e.g., "Summarize" or "Do’s and Don’ts"), the input text (pasted by the user) will be sent to ChatGPT's API. The ChatGPT result will be displayed below the input text area within the same pop-up window.
  6. Backend and API Call:
    • Step 6: The back-end server should handle the API call to OpenAI, sending the selected text along with the chosen prompt to get a result. The result is then displayed in the ChatGPT response area inside the modal window.
  7. Managing Prompts:
    • Step 7: For managing prompts:
      • Include a feature to allow users to add prompts to the list, which is then stored on the server.
      • Admins should have the ability to edit or delete prompts from the list, using a role-based access control mechanism.

 

 

 

=============================

 

Example Chain-of-Thought Process:

  1. User selects text: They highlight a paragraph in the editor.
  2. Click AI icon: A pop-up appears with two sections.
    • Section 1: Text input area (they manually paste the selected text).
    • Section 2: List of prompts (e.g., "Summarize," "Do's and Don'ts").
  3. User selects a prompt: They choose “Summarize.”
  4. ChatGPT processes: The server sends the text and prompt to ChatGPT via API.
  5. Result displayed: ChatGPT’s summary is shown below the text input area in the pop-up.

Clarifications/Final Adjustments:

  • Text area size: Do you want a fixed size for the input and output areas, or should they be resizable?
  • Prompt behavior: Should the selected prompt automatically disappear after the result is shown, or should it remain highlighted?

Once you confirm these, I can help finalize the prompt for the best implementation.

================

 

 

 

==================================

Additional info I asked

1) Backend Setup:

You already have a backend server, so let's discuss how best to structure it to support this new feature.

Key Considerations:

  • API Handling: Your backend needs to act as the intermediary between the frontend and the OpenAI API. It should receive text and prompt data, process it, and return the response.
  • Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Since you require different functionalities for users (adding prompts) and admins (editing/deleting prompts), RBAC is crucial. You can use libraries like JWT (JSON Web Tokens) for handling authentication and role-based permissions.

Recommendations:

  • Framework: I suggest using Node.js with Express if you're looking for a highly scalable solution in JavaScript/TypeScript environments. If you prefer Python, FastAPI is a good choice due to its speed and compatibility with AI-related tasks.
  • Security: Ensure proper API rate-limiting, especially with the ChatGPT API, to avoid overuse or misuse. Use libraries like express-rate-limit (Node) or SlowAPI (FastAPI) to manage this.

Backend Logic:

  • Upon receiving a request (selected text + chosen prompt), the backend should format the text and prompt into an API call to ChatGPT.
  • Parse the response and send it back to the frontend for display in the modal window.

Example Code Structure (Node.js + Express):

js

Copy code

const express = require('express'); const { Configuration, OpenAIApi } = require('openai'); const app = express(); const configuration = new Configuration({  apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY, }); const openai = new OpenAIApi(configuration); app.post('/chatgpt', async (req, res) => {  try {    const { selectedText, promptType } = req.body;    const prompt = generatePrompt(promptType, selectedText);    const response = await openai.createCompletion({      model: "gpt-3.5-turbo",      prompt: prompt,      max_tokens: 1000,    });    res.json(response.data.choices[0].text);  } catch (error) {    res.status(500).send('Error interacting with ChatGPT API');  } }); function generatePrompt(type, text) {  switch (type) {    case 'summary':      return `Summarize this: ${text}`;    case 'dos_donts':      return `Give me do's and don'ts for this: ${text}`;    default:      return text;  } }

2) Database:

You'll need a database to store user prompts, admin rights, and logs for queries to ChatGPT.

Recommendations:

  • Database Choice: For storing the prompts and user/admin data, a lightweight SQL database like SQLite or PostgreSQL would be a great fit for structured data. If you’re anticipating rapid scaling, go for PostgreSQL.
  • Tables:
    1. Prompts Table: Contains the custom prompts added by users/admins.
    2. User Table: Holds information about users and their roles (admin or regular user).
    3. Log Table: Tracks each interaction with ChatGPT (timestamp, text, prompt type, user ID). This is useful for auditing or debugging.

Example Table Structure (PostgreSQL):

sql

Copy code

CREATE TABLE prompts (    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,    user_id INT,    prompt TEXT,    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ); CREATE TABLE users (    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,    username VARCHAR(100),    role VARCHAR(50), -- either 'user' or 'admin'    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ); CREATE TABLE logs (    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,    user_id INT,    query TEXT,    result TEXT,    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP );

  • Prompts Management: When a user adds a new prompt, it is stored in the prompts table, and when an admin edits or deletes a prompt, the table is updated accordingly.

3) Frontend Setup:

In React, you’ll have to focus on building the modal window and handling user interactions efficiently.

Key Components:

  • Text Editor Component: This is where users write or select the text. Use Draft.js or Slate.js for a rich-text editor with customization options for the toolbar.
  • AI Button: You can add the AI button by extending the toolbar of your editor. This will trigger the modal window.
  • Modal Window: Use React libraries like Material-UI or Ant Design for building the modal pop-up with the two sections (ChatGPT and Prompts List).
  • State Management: You can use React Context or Redux to manage prompts, user roles, and ChatGPT API responses.

Frontend Workflow:

  1. The user selects text → clicks the AI button.
  2. A modal pops up with:
    • A text input area where they can paste or edit the selected text.
    • A list of prompts, which users can add to (admins can edit or delete).
  3. The selected prompt sends a request to the backend (API) with the text.

Example Structure (React + Hooks):

jsx

Copy code

const AiModal = ({ selectedText, closeModal }) => {  const [inputText, setInputText] = useState(selectedText || '');  const [result, setResult] = useState('');  const [prompts, setPrompts] = useState(['Give me a summary', 'Do\'s and Don\'ts']);  const handleSubmit = async (prompt) => {    const response = await fetch('/chatgpt', {      method: 'POST',      body: JSON.stringify({ selectedText: inputText, promptType: prompt }),    });    const resultText = await response.text();    setResult(resultText);  };  return (    <div className="ai-modal">      <textarea value={inputText} onChange={(e) => setInputText(e.target.value)} />      <div>        {prompts.map((prompt) => (          <button key={prompt} onClick={() => handleSubmit(prompt)}>            {prompt}          </button>        ))}      </div>      <div className="result">        <p>{result}</p>      </div>      <button onClick={closeModal}>Close</button>    </div>  ); };

4) API Development:

You’ll primarily use the OpenAI API to interface with ChatGPT, so the API development aspect is focused on making sure this interaction is seamless.

Key Features:

  • API Key Management: Your backend should securely store the OpenAI API key. You can use environment variables for this purpose (process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY).
  • Error Handling: Ensure the backend handles potential API rate limits and errors gracefully, returning user-friendly error messages to the frontend.

Rate Limiting:

To avoid overloading your OpenAI usage, you might consider limiting how often users can request summaries or analyses within a given time frame.

5) PDF Handling:

If you're working with PDFs (e.g., exporting the ChatGPT responses or selected text as PDFs), here's how to approach it:

PDF Export:

  • Use a library like jsPDF or pdf-lib on the frontend to generate PDFs from the content in the text editor or from the ChatGPT output.

Example for PDF Export (jsPDF):

js

Copy code

import jsPDF from 'jspdf'; const exportToPdf = (text) => {  const doc = new jsPDF();  doc.text(20, 20, text);  doc.save('output.pdf'); };

  • Backend Option: If you need server-side PDF generation, pdfkit in Node.js would be a good option for creating PDFs with more complex layouts or dynamic content.

Summary:

  • Backend: Use Node.js with Express for API handling and role-based access.
  • Database: Use PostgreSQL to manage prompts, users, and logging interactions.
  • Frontend: React for a rich-text editor with modal functionality for AI interaction.
  • API Development: Interface with OpenAI’s API securely and implement rate-limiting.
  • PDF Handling: Use jsPDF or pdf-lib for client-side PDF generation or pdfkit for backend generation.

From David:

Currently when in TASK we click on the + template we get very unorganized list ( see picture ) . We need to change this to as follow 

1- a Figma by River  based on the following:

2 - The Key Features:

  1. Template Library:
    • The template library should be organized by up to  as many  categories, each potentially containing up to as many  subcategories, with support for nested subcategories.
    • Users should be able to view all categories/subcategories in a managed way if they cannot find what they need.
  2. User Permissions:
    • There are two user roles:
      • Management Admin: Can access and edit all templates and manage all categories/subcategories.
      • General User: Can only access permitted templates and cannot see categories or subcategories that they are not allowed to view.
  3. Search and Filter Capabilities:
    • Full-text search across both the template title and contents.
    • Templates should include metadata, like date of creation and author.
    • Users should be able to filter templates by categories, subcategories, date, and author.
  4. Template Insertion Flow:
    • A pop-up window should be used to guide users through selecting the Category and Subcategory.
    • Once a template is selected, there should be an option for a preview before inserting it.
    • Users should be able to adjust variables or placeholders (e.g., customer name) during the insertion process.
    • Templates should be editable after insertion since they will be placed directly into the text editor.
  5. Integration with Text Editor:
    • The inserted template should automatically take on any existing styles or formatting of the text within the editor.

 

 

Optimized Prompt for Claude

Here’s an optimized prompt that can be given to developers or used to implement the features using an AI tool:

 

Prompt: "Create a Template Library feature for an existing text editor. The Template Library must have the following capabilities:

  1. Organization & Structure:
    • Templates are organized by up to as many as  categories, each containing  as many as  subcategories.
    • Support for nested subcategories should be provided, with an option for users to browse all categories and subcategories in a well-structured, managed interface if they can't find what they need.
  2. User Permissions:
    • Implement two user roles:
      • Management Admin: Can access and edit all templates, manage categories, and modify subcategories.
      • General User: Can only access templates they are permitted to view. They cannot see categories or subcategories that are restricted to them.
  3. Search & Filter:
    • Allow users to search templates with a full-text search that includes both template titles and contents.
    • Enable filtering based on categories, subcategories, date created, and author.
    • Each template should have metadata including date of creation and author.
  4. Template Selection & Insertion:
    • When adding a template to the editor, display a pop-up window prompting users to select a Category and Subcategory.
    • Show a subject list of templates for the chosen category/subcategory, and provide an option to preview the template.
    • During insertion, allow users to adjust placeholders/variables (e.g., customer name) to tailor the template before final insertion.
    • Templates, once inserted into the editor, should be editable as per the editor’s native functionality.
  5. Editor Integration:
    • Ensure that the inserted template inherits the existing styles and formatting of the text within the editor, so that the content maintains visual consistency.
  6. Additional Features:
    • Users should be able to add new categories and subcategories (restricted to Management Admin).
    • The UI for selecting templates should allow for an intuitive and user-friendly navigation system, especially considering the high number of categories and subcategories.

The overall goal is to provide a seamless user experience for inserting templates, with appropriate access control and editable options that enhance productivity while maintaining the structure and style consistency of the editor."

577.content:
We will have a transfer functionality that allows one to convert a OneSnap into a floor plan in a site. In order to do so, this process would be followed:

1. On desktop only, open a OneSnap

2. Go tp the gallery with all photos

3. In the upper right, there will be a "Transfer" button. Click this to open a pop up that covers the whole page.

4. The upper left section of this pop up will have all of the gallery photos

5. The lower left will contain the GPS map of all the photos that were taken, and can be collapsed/hidden just like on mobile onesurvey.

6. The right side will contain a section where someone can upload and scale a floor plan. drop a file in this area, or click to select from the device

          a. Add soon as someone drops a file here or uploads it, it lets the user scale it and enter a title

7. below the floor plan, would be a row of all of the quick elements.

          a. By default, the not element would be there

          b. There would also be a '+' icon to add new quick elements. Clicking this would slide up a menu to add more quick elements.

8. In the upper right above the floor plan, we need the option to rotate, crop, or resize the floor plan.

          a. Rotate: the user can click this icon, and it would let them rotate the floor plan by 90 degrees, and the user can click done once it is set.

          b. Crop: the user can click this icon to crop the floor plan without showing a pop up window like pintura photo editor. The crop functionality should be built into the app.

          c. Resize: clicking this icon would allow the user to adjust the scaling of the floor plan. Like the other 2, this will not be a pop up window.

9. The user should NOT be able to drag and drop any icons or any pictures until a floor plan is uploaded and scaled.

10. Icons can be dragged and dropped from the bottom menu onto the floor plan (no FoV or other fancy OneSurvey options available here)

11. Once the icons are dragged and dropped, the pictures from the upper left can be dragged and dropped onto and icon

12. The pictures can be added 1x1, or multi select first then dragged and dropped in bulk into one icon.

          a. For multiselect: make it so we can just hover over and click the circular icon to select multiple, instead of needing to click a select button first.

          b. Once pictures are dragged into an icon, they no longer appear on the upper left gallery section

To embed ChatGPT and its API into your Note-to-Task Engine for dynamic note searching, and allow for enhanced interaction with your notes, you can follow these steps:
 

( Tasked by David to Affandy ) 

1. Integrate ChatGPT API into Your App

  • First, you’ll need to connect to the OpenAI API (or whichever version of ChatGPT you prefer). If you’re already familiar with Python or React (as mentioned in your previous communications), this can be done by making requests to the ChatGPT API.

Example in Python:

python

Copy code

import openai

# Set up OpenAI API Key
openai.api_key = 'your_openai_api_key'

def search_notes_with_gpt(query, notes):
    response = openai.ChatCompletion.create(
      model="gpt-4",
      messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": f"Search the following notes for: {query}\n{notes}"}
      ]
    )
    return response['choices'][0]['message']['content']

# Example note data
notes = [
    {"content": "Meeting notes from 10/10 about AI integration."},
    {"content": "Task for 10/11 about security system setup."}
]

query = "AI integration"
search_results = search_notes_with_gpt(query, notes)
print(search_results)
 

2. Set Up Dynamic Connections

To make dynamic connections between the notes in your app and ChatGPT, you can:

  • Convert your existing note data (content, tags, hotkeys, etc.) into a format that ChatGPT can process (like JSON).
  • Send the data to ChatGPT through API calls whenever you perform a search.
  • Dynamically retrieve results by having ChatGPT return relevant notes or summaries based on your query.

Steps:

  1. Create an API Layer:
    Set up a layer between your app and the ChatGPT API that takes user input (search queries) and the content of your notes. This layer can handle queries dynamically and call ChatGPT as needed.
  2. Query Specific Notes:
    Let’s say you want to search specific notes or a group of notes. You can send the content of these notes to ChatGPT along with the user’s query. For example:
    • If you search for “AI integration” in the note’s content, ChatGPT will process the search and highlight relevant results.

3. Create a ChatGPT-powered Search Feature

You can enhance your search and filter functions by adding a ChatGPT-powered feature that:

  • Allows users to input natural language queries like "Find notes about AI integration from last month."
  • Filters dynamically using your hotkeys, tags, and priority levels but with ChatGPT’s more flexible search capabilities.

Example:

You can build an input field in your app's interface that accepts natural language queries:

python

Copy code

user_query = "Find all notes related to AI in progress"

response = openai.ChatCompletion.create(
    model="gpt-4",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a note manager."},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_query}
    ]
)
 

ChatGPT can then filter through the list of notes and return the most relevant ones.

4. Advanced Features

  • Summarization: You can add the ability for ChatGPT to summarize a large set of notes, giving you a high-level overview of everything under a specific hotkey or tag.
  • Categorization: ChatGPT can automatically suggest tags or categories for new notes by analyzing their content.

5. Refine Search and Interaction

  • Contextual search: ChatGPT can provide context-based results. For instance, if you're looking for notes with a specific context (e.g., “AI projects from last week”), it can return filtered results with relevant time frames or content.
  • Ask ChatGPT specific questions: Once embedded, you can ask ChatGPT to perform more complex searches, such as, “Show me all notes with high priority tasks related to AI integration.”

6. UI/UX Consideration

In your app’s interface:

  • Add a ChatGPT search bar where users can type queries in natural language.
  • The search results can be dynamically populated in a panel with interactive filtering options for users to fine-tune the results further.
  • You can also allow users to ask clarifying questions about the search results (“What tasks are overdue from last week?”).

7. Next Steps

  • API Key Management: Store your OpenAI API key securely in your app, and manage rate limits based on your usage.
  • Optimize Data Passing: When sending note content to ChatGPT, ensure you pass only relevant notes or use metadata to keep interactions efficient.
  • Test and Adjust: As you integrate, test how well ChatGPT retrieves and filters your notes. You may need to tweak the prompts or instructions for optimal results.

By embedding ChatGPT in this manner, you can make your note searches far more intuitive and interactive, saving time and improving efficiency.
